Fundamental Symmetries

A little rigor

Discrete Symmetries in Nature

  1. Charge conjugation, C: Pion Decay
  2. Parity (mirror reflection), P: Weak force, e.g. neutron β decay
  3. Time reversal, T: Kaon decay

$$\eta > \eta_\mathrm{SM} = 0$$

You can talk about combined symmetries:
CPT is Lorentz invariant, so CP=T

EDM Violates Several Symmetries

  C P T
$\phantom{\mu\hat{J}\cdot}\vec{B}$ - + -
$\phantom{\mu\hat{J}\cdot}\hat{J}$ - + -
$\mu\hat{J}\cdot\vec{B}$ + + +
  C P T
$\phantom{d\hat{J}\cdot}\vec{E}$ - - +
$\phantom{d\hat{J}\cdot}\hat{J}$ - + -
$d\hat{J}\cdot\vec{E}$ + - -
$$\mathcal{H} = \mu\hat{J}\cdot\vec{B} + d\hat{J}\cdot\vec{E}$$

Which Symmetries are "good" Symmetries?

1950 Parity (mirror) symmetry was believed to be conserved.
1956 Lee and Yang: P is not tested in weak force
Jan 1957 Madame Wu observes P violation in neutron β decay
May 1957 Smith, Purcell, Ramsey publish null nEDM
1964 Cronin and Fitch observe CP violation in neutral Kaon

  1. $\alpha$: polarization*analyzing power
  2. T: precession time
  3. E: Electric field strength
  4. N: observed particle number

Ultra-Cold Neutrons (UCN)

  • milliKelvin "temperature"
  • <300 neV
  • Extremely slow neutrons
  • $v > $ 5–8 m/s
  • $\lambda>$ 50 nm
  • Neutron + Gravity: 102 neV/m
  • Neutron + Magnetism: 60 neV/T
  • Benefits?
  • Long storage time (β limited)
  • Low radiation background
  • 100% polarization

Systematics

zero v zero problems?

Reducing $\vec{v}$ increases observation time and improves $B'\approx B - \frac{\vec{v}\times\vec{E}}{c^2}$

Bottled neutrons $\langle\vec{v}\rangle = 0\quad \stackrel{?}{\Rightarrow}\quad \langle\vec{v}\times\vec{E}\rangle=0$?

Magnetic Field Gradients: $\nabla\cdot\vec{B}=0$   so   $\partial_x B_x+ \partial_y B_y+ \partial_z B_z = 0$

Some math happens: $\delta\omega\propto E \partial_z B_z$

Experimental Signal: $\delta\omega = \frac{4d_nE}{h}$

Gradient Specification

  • Scalar Potential
  • Stream-functions
$$d_{\mathrm{Hg}\to n}^{\mathrm{false}}=-\frac{\hbar |\gamma_n\gamma_{\mathrm{Hg}}|}{2c^2}\sum\limits_{l,m} G_{l,m}\langle\rho \Pi_{\rho,l,m}\rangle$$ $$\frac{1}{T_{2,\mathrm{mag}}}=\gamma_n^2\sum\limits_{l,l',m}G_{l,m}G_{l',m}\int_0^\infty\langle \Pi_{z,l,m}^c(0)\Pi_{z,l',m}^c(t)\rangle\,\mathrm{d}t$$

Stream Functions via bfieldTools

From the theory of harmonic potentials, we know that U can be determined uniquely in the volume (up to a constant) when either the potential or the normal derivative of the potential is specified on the boundary enclosing the volume. Thus, any external source distribution whose potential reproduces the boundary conditions of a given U, can be used to generate U in the volume. —Mäkinen
